newsitem.title: UK: Trade gap widens as buyers lap up imports.
newsitem.headline: Trade gap widens as buyers lap up imports.

text.p: Britain's trade deficit grew 9 percent in July as a consumer-led economic recovery sucked in more goods than were sold abroad, official figures showed Thursday.

The Office for National Statistics said the global trade deficit widened to 1.23 billion pounds ($1.92 billion) from 1.13 billion pounds ($1.76 billion) in June. The deficit was distinctly larger than forecast. Financial analysts had expected the trade gap to narrow to about 775 million pounds ($1.21 billion).
The government shrugged off the report, saying it was evidence of the competitive strength of the British economy.

"This is another set of figures confirming the competitive strength of the UK economy...UK exporters are in an ideal position to benefit from the upturn in our key European markets," Treasury minister Angela Knight said.
The 1.0 percent jump in imports in July was largely due to consumption of consumer goods from overseas. Demand for clothing from the Far East was a key factor, the office said.
Analysts said with consumer spending likely to accelerate, demand for imports would probably rise further later this year.
"The import side is a source of some concern. It's another sign demand for consumer goods is accelerating," said Alex Garrard, economist at UBS.
The trade gap could also come under pressure from higher demand for capital and intermediate goods as the recovery in manufacturing gathers speed.
On the export side, sluggish demand for British goods in the European Union was largely responsible for a tiny 0.3 percent rise in overall sales of British goods abroad in July.
Sharper demand for imports in Europe had been expected to follow the tentative signs of an economic upturn in those economies.
